title: News 12 reporter flies in Blue Angels F/A-18, pulling more than seven Gs - WCTI
content: The highlight of the Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point Air Show is the Navy Blue Angels team. They are elite aviators who demonstrate the skill and stamina needed to fly some of the world’s fastest jets. I had the honor of flying along with them in the back seat of an F/A-18. News 12 reporter flies in Blue Angels F/A-18, pulling more than seven Gs The day started early Wednesday morning with a flight briefing from the Blue Angels crew chief for community key influencer Holly Tolsten and me. He prepared us for what to expect in one of the Navy’s fastest and most maneuverable fighter jets — the F/A-18. News 12 reporter flies in Blue Angels F/A-18, pulling more than seven Gs We practiced bracing for high G-forces and breathing techniques to avoid passing out during aggressive maneuvers. News 12 reporter flies in Blue Angels F/A-18, pulling more than seven Gs After getting fitted with flight suits and helmets, Holly was up first. She was selected as the community key influencer from several candidates. She serves as the Career and Technical Education Coordinator for Craven County Schools. News 12 reporter flies in Blue Angels F/A-18, pulling more than seven Gs Lieutenant Ronny Haveza was at the controls of Blue Angel 7. After a little more than 30 minutes in the air, Holly landed safely and was grateful for the experience. News 12 reporter flies in Blue Angels F/A-18, pulling more than seven Gs Lieutenant Haveza started off with a high-performance takeoff — going from zero to 10,000 feet in just seconds. We spent more than 40 minutes in the air, at one point pulling more than seven Gs — that’s seven times my body weight. Back on the ground, I have a newfound appreciation for what these elite aviators do every day.

South Simcoe Police say the robbery unfolded at the 400 Market, located on Industrial Park Rd. north of Innisfil Beach Rd., around 9:15 a.m. “Initial information indicated that six suspects arrived in a light-coloured van and stole approximately $300,000 worth of merchandise from the victim,” police said in a statement. Police said officers later located the suspect vehicle, identified as a 2008 blue Toyota Sienna, abandoned in a lot at Innisfil Beach Rd. and Industrial Park Rd. – a short distance from where the robbery occurred. Investigators obtained video from a nearby security camera and have released an image from the footage hoping members of the public recognize the six unidentified bandits and come forward. The suspected driver of the getaway vehicle is described as wearing a black baseball cap, blue medical mask, white-collared jacket and black joggers. The second suspect was wearing a black hooded sweatshirt, blue medical mask and black joggers. The third suspect was wearing a black hat, blue medical mask, black hoodie with white design on the shoulders and back, and black joggers. The fourth was wearing a black baseball cap, blue medical mask, black coat and black joggers. The fifth was wearing a white hat, blue medical mask, blue coat and grey joggers. The sixth suspect was wearing a black hat, blue medical mask, black coat and blue jeans. “This incident appears to be isolated and there is no ongoing risk to public safety,” police said, adding the investigation is “ongoing.” Anyone with information regarding the identity of any of the six thieves, or video that could help investigators, is urged to call police 905-775-3311, ext. 1461 or Crime Stoppers anonymously at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). title: BMW F450 GS review: Big-bike GS feel in a LAMS package - Bike Rider Magazine
content: BMW’s new F450 GS brings premium electronics, parallel-twin performance and genuine off-road ability to the LAMS adventure class — but does the badge justify the higher price? BMW has finally entered the booming LAMS adventure segment with the all-new BMW F450 GS — a lightweight parallel-twin designed to bring proper GS styling and premium features to newer riders. First shown in concept form before breaking cover at EICMA, the F450 GS arrives with a new 420cc twin-cylinder engine, 48hp, 135-degree crank, lean-sensitive electronics, long-travel suspension and BMW’s unusual Easy Ride Clutch system. The chassis is fresh too, featuring a steel-tube frame, KYB suspension and 19/17-inch wheels. And with 180mm travel and 220mm ground clearance, it’s built to leave the tarmac. Built in partnership with TVS in India, it’s positioned as the replacement for the single-cylinder G310 GS, but with far more performance and significantly more spec. “It feels every bit like a proper GS — just scaled down for newer riders.” BMW says the F450 GS has been developed specifically to appeal to newer riders stepping into adventure bikes, while still offering enough performance and capability to satisfy experienced riders wanting a lightweight all-rounder. In New Zealand, pricing starts at $13,490 + ORC for the Exclusive model, climbing to $14,490 + ORC for the GS Trophy variant. The question is simple: does BMW’s smallest GS deserve the badge? Chad headed to a very wet Sicily to put the newest GS to the test. Interest was huge when the F450 GS broke cover in Milan in 2024. Since then, it’s felt like a long wait. In Sicily, finally, it lands — and it delivers. The Trophy, with its white frame and spoked wheels, looks every inch a junior GS. Think scaled-down F900 GS. Proper family resemblance. Built in India with TVS Motor Company, NZ pricing starts at $13,490 + ORC for the Exclusive Cosmic Black model. The Sport Racing Red costs $13,890 + ORC, while the GS Trophy comes in at $14,490 + ORC. Despite the ‘entry-level’ positioning of the new GS, the spec is still strong. The 6.5-inch TFT is lifted straight from bigger GS models, complete with BMW’s familiar switchgear and rotary controller. Heated grips come standard, and overall quality feels genuinely premium for the class. Electronics back that up. Multiple riding modes, lean-sensitive ABS and traction control, plus wheelie and engine brake control all feature. Add the Easy Ride Clutch and, at around $14k, the BMW is loaded compared to most rivals. On board, it feels like a bigger GS. Quality is high. Gold handlebars add a touch of class, while the optional suspension brings adjustability. We started off-road on the Trophy, ERC fitted, then switched to the Sport on tarmac. First hurdle: moving off. The Easy Ride Clutch is BMW trying something genuinely different. It’s a centrifugal setup that allows the bike to pull away without traditional clutch control — almost scooter-like at low speed. No need for the lever when moving off from a standstill. Initially, it feels odd. Then it quickly becomes intuitive. Once rolling, you still shift gears normally, especially with the optional quickshifter fitted. “The Easy Ride Clutch genuinely changes the riding experience.” It’s clever. New riders won’t stall it, and off-road it frees up your left hand while removing the need for delicate clutch work. It’s not perfect — there’s a slight disconnect in feel, and you can’t “park in gear” on hills — but as a confidence-building feature, it works extremely well. Sicily’s tight, cobbled streets showed the BMW’s softer side. Easy, relaxed, almost scooter-like in traffic. The electronics keep things tidy on slippery surfaces, and the bike feels unintimidating from the first few metres. Performance is solid for a LAMS machine. The new 420cc twin produces 48hp and 43Nm, with most of the torque arriving low in the rev range. BMW’s 135-degree crank promises added character, though on the road it feels broadly similar to other parallel twins. No fireworks, just usable drive. Still, there’s enough poke to lift the front wheel in lower gears, and the bike feels lively enough to stay entertaining. Cruising at motorway speeds is easy enough, though wind protection is average and there’s no cruise control. Fuel economy looks impressive, with BMW claiming 3.8L/100km and potential range pushing close to 320km from the 14-litre tank. The brakes lacked feel in the wet conditions we experienced, but the chassis remained composed and the rider aids worked seamlessly. Manageable, forgiving and lighter than its numbers suggest, it quickly builds rider confidence. The Metzeler Karoo 4 tyres on our Trophy-spec bike found grip almost everywhere, while Enduro Plus mode happily allowed the rear to slide around. Suspension performance is impressive considering the target market. The KYB setup copes well with rough terrain, although aggressive riders will eventually find the limits. Still, I reckon it’s one of the easiest adventure bikes in the class to ride off-road. The Easy Ride Clutch helps here too. Removing the need for constant clutch work makes technical riding noticeably less intimidating for newer riders. Back on the road, even with aggressive tyres fitted, the bike remained composed. Switch to the Sport model and it instantly feels familiar — proper GS DNA, simply scaled back. A few questions remain. We still need dry-road testing, higher-speed touring evaluation and a proper assessment of vibration levels over longer distances. But one thing is already obvious: BMW’s smallest GS makes a very strong first impression. With 48hp and 178kg wet, it sits right on the edge of LAMS regulations while offering class-leading performance. The new 420cc twin is easy, usable and entertaining enough to keep experienced riders interested. Add the Easy Ride Clutch and it arguably becomes the most accessible adventure bike in the segment, both on and off road. Pricing will divide opinion. Some riders will expect it to be cheaper. Others will accept the BMW premium, especially given the level of finish and equipment. Even the base bike gets BMW’s full-fat TFT display, premium switchgear and lean-sensitive electronics. Add a few options and it becomes one of the most comprehensively equipped bikes in the class. But rivals such as the KTM 390 Adventure, CFMOTO 450MT and Royal Enfield Himalayan 450 undercut it significantly on price. There are niggles too. No “park in gear” functionality with the Easy Ride Clutch, average wind protection and a few unanswered questions after a rain-soaked launch test. Even so, there’s a strong argument that BMW has produced the best LAMS adventure bike currently available. It looks the part, delivers serious spec and is ridiculously easy to ride. “It looks the part, delivers serious spec and builds confidence quickly.” The real question is whether newer riders will pay the premium for the badge. title: This Spider Launches at 130 G’s (Humans Black Out at 9) - AOL.com
content: Some predators chase. Others ambush. And then there are the ones that shoot. Across the animal kingdom, a surprising number of species have evolved ways to hit prey from a distance — firing water jets, venom sprays, sticky silk, or even microscopic harpoons. These aren’t gimmicks. They’re highly specialized hunting systems designed to solve one core problem: how to catch prey that is faster than the predator. Many rely on what scientists call latch-mediated spring actuation (LaMSA) — a way to store energy and release it instantly, like a biological trigger. The result is explosive speed, extreme precision, and in some cases, forces that rival human-made machines. From fish that snipe insects out of the air to snails that fire venom-loaded harpoons, these predators have weaponized the laws of physics. While many creatures, such as bombardier beetles and spitting cobras, “shoot” to defend themselves, these elite marksmen use their abilities offensively, actively hunting and capturing their next meal. If you thought fish only hunted underwater, the archerfish will quickly prove you wrong. This aquatic outlaw can knock insects off branches up to 5 feet above the water by firing a precise jet of water from its mouth. But it’s not just about force or power; it’s about physics and precision. Because light bends when it passes from air to water, the fish’s view of the insect is distorted. To hit its mark, the archerfish must account for this “refraction” before firing. This skill isn’t purely instinctual, either. Young archerfish practice to refine their aim, eventually achieving near-perfect accuracy, especially when they position themselves directly beneath their target. While many spiders wait for prey to get stuck in their webs, the spitting spider actively immobilizes its prey. In a fraction of a second, the spider sprays a specialized mixture of liquid silk and venom from its fangs while it rapidly vibrates its head, causing the silky streams to form a zigzagging net in the air. This sticky, toxic mesh pins insects to whatever surface they’re on. It’s fast, precise, and extremely effective. Unlike other eight-eyed spider species, spitting spiders only have six eyes. While most shrimp are scavengers, the pistol shrimp is a gunslinger of the sea. Unlike its relatives, this impressive hunter doesn’t kill by pinching; it uses physics to hunt. When the shrimp slams its oversized claw shut, it ejects a high-speed jet of water that creates a cavitation bubble. This bubble is a tiny pocket of low pressure that collapses almost instantly, triggering a massive release of energy. The pistol shrimp may only be 1.5 inches long, but it can move its claws at 60 miles per hour. The collapse of this bubble is so violent that it produces a shockwave louder than a gunshot, stunning or killing small prey from a distance. For a tiny fraction of a second, the temperature inside the collapsing bubble can reach nearly 8,700 degrees Fahrenheit (4,800 degrees Celsius). The energy release is so intense it actually produces a brief flash of light. The shrimp’s claw features a unique spiral, crack-resistant structure designed to withstand the repeated stress of these underwater “explosions.” Materials scientists are actively studying the pistol shrimp’s claw to develop stronger, more impact-resistant armor and helmets for humans. The velvet worm may appear soft, slow, and relatively harmless, but it is a surprisingly effective predator. Using specialized nozzles near its mouth, it sprays twin jets of slime at a speed reaching nearly 5 feet per second. The slime hardens in the air as the jets oscillate rapidly, and the movement ensures that the slimy webbing covers a large area to make it nearly impossible for an insect to escape. Once its prey is immobilized, the worm dissolves the victim’s insides and consumes the liquefied remains. Velvet worms typically hunt woodlice, crickets, and spiders. The worm also eats the dried strands of slime afterward, ensuring that no resources are wasted after the energy-intensive hunt. Unlike other spiders that build stationary webs and wait for prey to get caught, the ogre-faced spider actively casts its net like a tiny eight-legged fisherman. Hanging upside down from a single silk line, the spider holds a small, rectangular frame of highly elastic silk between its front legs. It uses its specialized slit sensilla or vibration sensors to detect the movements of insects walking or flying nearby. When an insect comes within range, the spider lunges, stretching the net to several times its original size and snapping it over the prey. Two of the ogre-faced spider’s eyes face forward and are much bigger than the rest, giving it excellent low-light night vision. The cone snail moves at a literal snail’s pace, yet its strike is one of the fastest and most lethal in nature. Instead of chasing its prey, this snail uses its hollow, venom-tipped tooth—essentially a built-in biological harpoon—to strike with incredible speed. It happens in less than one millisecond, even faster than the blink of a human eye. Once the harpoon hits, the snail injects a complex cocktail of neurotoxins that shuts down the prey’s nervous system instantly. Some cone snail species can launch their harpoon in less than 100 microseconds. Some species, like the geography cone (Conus geographus), are so toxic that a single sting can be fatal to humans. This species is sometimes called the “cigarette snail” due to a grim myth: if you are stung, you’ll only have enough time to smoke one last cigarette before you die. While this may be an exaggeration, the venom does act extremely quickly. Instead of spinning traditional webs, the bolas spider uses a specialized “fishing” technique to catch its prey. Instead of a net, it creates a single silk line tipped with a heavy and sticky glob called a bolas. The bolas’ incredibly sticky texture allows it to bypass a moth’s slippery scales and adhere directly to its body. The bolas spider creates silk with a sticky texture. ©Judy Gallagher / CC BY 2.0 / Wikimedia Commons – Original / License The spider releases a scent that mimics the pheromones of a female moth. When a male moth approaches in search of a mate, the spider swings the bolas in a circular motion to snag the moth out of the air. The chameleon is a long-range predator that relies on mechanical advantage rather than raw muscle power to catch its prey. Its long tongue doesn’t simply reach out to snatch up an insect; instead, the chameleon launches it from its mouth like a high-speed projectile. This mechanism relies on stored energy rather than rapid muscle movement, allowing it to function even in cooler temperatures. Chameleons have a unique physiology that allows them to “wind up” energy in their tongue’s tissue so they can snap it out at speeds of 60 miles per hour in a fraction of a second. The tip of the chameleon’s tongue has a suction cup-like pouch coated with saliva that is about 400 times thicker than human saliva. This special coating ensures that the bond is strong enough to pull the prey back, even if it is heavy or struggling. Rather than waiting for an insect to fly into its web, the slingshot spider transforms its entire web into a loaded spring. It constructs a conical web and pulls the center tight using a tension line attached to a nearby surface. By pulling back and holding the web under extreme tension, the spider stores potential energy, essentially turning itself into a living bow and arrow. When the spider senses prey, it releases the tension line, sending itself and its web catapulting forward at over 130 Gs (for perspective, humans typically black out at around 9 Gs). The sudden launch collapses the web over the prey, entangling it before it can react. Slingshot spiders shoot their own bodies at their prey. ©LOPEZ André / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons – Original / License The same silk structures that provide the tension also act as shock absorbers, bringing the spider to a safe stop at the end of its flight. title: Test riding BMW F 450 GS: It will definitely make new riders very happy - Team-BHP
content: BHPian bblost recently shared this with other enthusiasts: There is hardly anything I can add to tell you how beautiful and well-balanced it looks. It’s purpose-built for tackling any kind of terrain that is thrown at it. It does not disappoint and lives up to its looks. There is an option to pay more money and get fancier wheels, but the default set is, in my honest opinion, quite acceptable. I rode the bike for about an hour. Most of it was on the narrow roads of Goa, where I did not cross 60 km/h. I also got to ride the bike on open ground. My daily rides are a Himalayan 411 and a Bear 650. My opinion of this BMW will definitely be colored through this lens. The BMW seat is in the sweet spot for my average height of about 5 feet 10 inches. I could easily flat-foot and balance it at a standstill. Getting on the bike is extremely easy, and I did not have to use the footpeg to mount it. This is something I almost always end up doing on my Himalayan. There is no main stand. The side stand is very sturdy, and the bike feels planted without making me nervous about it toppling over. The first time I sat on the bike, it was before anyone told me anything about its features. I started the bike, slotted it into first gear, and let go of the clutch. Nothing happened. The console clearly showed that the bike was in first gear. The clutch lever was free, the engine was humming, but the bike was not moving. I have rarely felt so lost on a motorcycle… Thankfully, I did not pull the accelerator hard. I slowly twisted it, and as it crossed 2700 rpm, the bike moved forward. Some guardian angel protected everyone in the parking lobby. Over the next day, as I rode the bike, I kind of understood why this is going to be the most debated feature on this bike. It definitely makes life easier. But in traffic, where we are used to half-clutching to keep crawling forward, this is where it will be put to the test. The bike is noisy. You mostly hear the engine, and for a twin, it’s not exactly enchanting. The few times I crossed 50 km/h, the sound did settle down and maybe at higher speeds it becomes much more tolerable. The engine has good power, and it pulls well. But with this Easy Clutch, it’s very easy to forget the gear it is in. A warning flashes, the bike feels weird, and you shift to the correct gear. This will take a little getting used to. The bike is very light. Coming from the world of Royal Enfields, this felt like a feather that reacts instantly and lets you go exactly where you want. But I did find taking a U-turn on a narrow road extremely challenging. Trying to control it using just the accelerator is not quite easy. The seat is awesome. It has a slight rise at just the right place. This keeps you planted correctly even when accelerating hard. By the time the event was over and the last few batches were taking off, I spent a few minutes checking out the bikes in the parking area. Quite a few of them had taken a hit. But while the body panels had quite a lot of scratches, I did not find anything broken or loose. The bike will definitely make new riders very happy. title: GS Caltex's One-Club Star Han Soo-jin Re-signs for Three Years - 조선일보
content: Championship libero prioritizes loyalty over offers from rival teams, extending 9-season tenure with 750 million won contract [Sports Chosun Kim Young-rok Reporter] "My first priority was my original team. Other teams contacted me, and I did meet with them, but..." While Giselle Silva is undoubtedly the MVP of GS Caltex's championship, there's another hero who steadfastly supported the team. She is Han Soo-jin, GS Caltex's 'championship libero.' Han Soo-jin became a free agent for the second time in her career this spring, three years after her first free agency in spring 2023. Han Soo-jin inked a three-year contract worth a total of 750 million Korean won with GS Caltex. "During my first free agency, my position wasn't clear, and I didn't play much. I wasn't a player who received much recognition. So I didn't have many choices. This time is different. Even with offers from other teams, my determination to stay with GS Caltex was strong." The V-League immediately begins the free agent battle as soon as the championship finals conclude. Han Soo-jin recalled, "There was a team that contacted me before GS Caltex." "I met the coach from that team at a café and talked for about an hour. We only discussed volleyball, and I couldn't even catch my breath during that time. I almost considered switching teams." However, Han Soo-jin's heart was already set on GS Caltex. She joined the team as the first overall pick in the 2017–2018 rookie draft and has played for nine seasons. Han Soo-jin smiled, saying, "The value of being a one-club player was most precious to me." With Ahn Hye-jin remaining an unsigned free agent, Han Soo-jin became the player who has worn the mint-green uniform the longest. If she completes her three-year contract, she will surpass Han Da-hye (Pepper Savings Bank, 11 seasons) to become the player with the longest tenure in the club's history. The glory of being the 'first overall pick' was actually a burden throughout Han Soo-jin's career. Though dubbed the 'Suwon volleyball prodigy' for her explosive athleticism, she stands at just 1.65 meters. Han Soo-jin herself recalls it as a shocking memory, saying, "I never imagined it. It felt like a dream." But now, it's a source of pride. Her draft classmates include setter Lee Won-jung (Pepper Savings Bank), outside hitter Kim Ju-hyang (GS Caltex), Woo Soo-min (unsigned), and middle blocker Kim Chae-yeon (Industrial Bank of Korea (IBK)). Kim Chae-yeon won Rookie of the Year in their first season, and setter Kim Da-in (Hyundai Engineering & Construction), picked 10th overall in the second round, might be considered the biggest success, but ultimately, GS Caltex's choice was correct. They were the only team that recognized a player worthy of the first overall pick. "Actually, I prepared to be a libero since high school because of my height. But due to my high school team's circumstances, I had to play multiple positions. I'm glad I had diverse experiences, but it was regrettable that I couldn't focus on one. I think I'm here today because I climbed up step by step from the bottom." Even after turning professional, there were many ups and downs. She started as a setter before switching to libero. Even after establishing herself as a libero, she faced criticism for having 'good digs but weak receives' and went through a period where she played in a two-libero system. Now, she has grown into a top-tier libero in the league, recognized by both herself and others. Behind Silva's powerful spikes are Han Soo-jin's full-body dives. As her nickname 'Power Soo-jin' suggests, she is undeniably GS Caltex's training king. She is also a passionate player who commands the court with her fiery voice. Han Soo-jin, the 'championship libero,' is perhaps the result of outstanding talent combined with consistent effort. GS Caltex continues its fourth year with Silva. Han Soo-jin said, "I want to win another championship next season while playing with Silva. I'll do my best," reaffirming her resolve.

title: Gen.G's pushing to build the next generation of gaming pros - Yahoo Sports
content: Imagine being a basketball player and believing that the only path to a career in basketball is to be a professional player. It’s an absurd notion in traditional sports — but it’s the perception problem facing esports today. Gen.G aims to help solve this problem. The organization, which fields competitive esports teams in Korea and North America, is looking to bridge the gap between the two regions by offering students from high school through college the opportunity to build gaming careers that go beyond players, coaches, and coding. “If you think about it, the majority of gamers say they’re interested in a career in games. The number is something like 70 percent,” Gen.G CEO Arnold Hur said. “But by the time they graduate college, less than one percent actually take a very specific course around specifically games.” In February, Gen.G partnered with Arizona State University’s GAME School to host a series of gaming-related courses during their Gen.G Gaming Career Summer Camp at ASU Los Angeles. The in-person courses run from June to August, ranging from one- to four-week-long cohorts. Prices range from $599 to $1,899, and registration is open until May 29. The courses cover topics such as business and monetization, marketing, social media and content creation, esports operations, events and media production, and AI, technology, and future careers in gaming. “If you look at where the jobs actually are, coding and game development is maybe 10, 15 percent of all the jobs in gaming,” Hur said. “Just the same way that if you want to work in fashion, being a fashion designer is a small fraction of all the jobs in fashion.” The summer camp is the latest offering that Gen.G presented to students in the United States. In October 2025, Gen.G partnered with universities, including the University of Hawaiʻi, to give students a chance to study esports in Korea, which features one of the healthiest esports and gaming ecosystems in the world. “In North America, you still have that gap in understanding,” said Dr. Nyle Sky Kauweloa, a professor at the University of Hawaiʻi. “There is sort of a one-shot, moonshot idea of going professional, and it’s kind of an all-stakes buy-in. With Gen.G, there is a realistic understanding that we have the one percents, but what do we do with the 99 percent that don’t make it? They are able to funnel those students into a different direction.” University of California, Irvine student Kylan Dao participated in the Gen.G study abroad program. He became one of the program’s student ambassadors after returning, opting to take advantage of an opportunity rarely available to students at the collegiate level. “There are so many people who want to get into the industry,” Dao said. “They just don’t know how, or they don’t know where to go. I was in that same position.” One of the things he noticed during his time in Korea was the numerous pathways students had to find careers in gaming. “One of the biggest differences is how culturally significant esports is,” Dao said. “They have so many different educational programs, going into middle school, high school. We don’t here in the United States realistically expose our students to these various roles.” While Gen.G isn’t the first and — more than likely — won’t be the last to attempt to implement esports education programs for students, it’s attempting to create a healthy career pathway for gamers to pursue their passions without the need to be a player or developer. “There are more good games than there are successful games,” Hur said. “Even if you have a great game, it’s almost impossible to be successful. That’s not enough. And there aren’t enough people teaching from the industry how to make a great game successful.” Paul Delos Santos covers esports for The Sporting Tribune. He is also the founder of Inside Esports, a newsletter covering the Fighting Game Community and Riot Games esports ecosystem. Subscribe at insideesports.media.

title: U.S. military senior NCOs: An untapped civil service advantage for GS-10 through GS-14 roles - Federal News Network
content:
Agencies consistently say they need employees who can lead with character, understand complex systems and get things done. Senior NCOs arrive with all three. The federal government frequently discusses workforce agility, succession planning, institutional knowledge loss and the need for experienced employees who can enter complex organizations and contribute immediately. Yet one of its most underused talent pools remains the United States military’s Senior Noncommissioned Officer (NCO) corps. Although veterans are hired across government every year, agencies often fail to deliberately recruit, translate and place senior NCOs into GS-10 through GS-14 civil service roles, where their experience aligns most naturally. This gap is less about lack of hiring authority and more about failure to recognize how closely senior NCO responsibilities already mirror federal mid-level work. This missed opportunity is most visible in positions requiring operational maturity, leadership, process discipline, training oversight, logistics coordination, inspections, policy execution and program management. These are not unfamiliar responsibilities to senior NCOs. They are central to how senior enlisted leaders serve across the U.S. military. Too often, however, hiring officials interpret military experience too narrowly, viewing senior NCOs mainly as tactical leaders or disciplinarians rather than as professionals who manage systems, enforce standards, supervise staff, synchronize resources and turn intent into execution. That narrow view misses the true scope of senior NCO service. Whether serving as First Sergeants, Master Sergeants, Sergeant Majors, or Command Sergeant Majors, senior NCOs are expected to preserve readiness, develop leaders, sustain accountability, maintain standards, identify organizational weaknesses and keep institutions functioning under pressure. Their work extends far beyond leading formations. It includes managing training programs, monitoring personnel readiness, inspecting compliance, synchronizing logistics, enforcing administrative systems and supporting commanders through disciplined execution. In civilian terms, this often resembles the daily work of management analysts, operations specialists, administrative officers, training managers, logistics professionals and first-line supervisors. This is why senior NCOs should be viewed not simply as veterans, but as institutional leaders. They understand that mission success depends not only on strategy, but on standards, systems, follow-through and people. They are trained by experience to recognize that a missed training event, incomplete personnel action, weak inspection program, poor maintenance process or breakdown in communication can create larger organizational failure. Senior NCOs learn to connect these issues as parts of a single system rather than as isolated tasks. That system’s mindset is exactly what many federal organizations need. Join us May 11 for Federal News Network's Risk & Compliance Exchange as government and industry experts discuss how to navigate evolving cybersecurity mandates and accelerate secure adoption of emerging technologies. The GS-10 through GS-13 range is especially important because it forms much of the federal government’s execution layer. These employees turn policy into performance. They serve as analysts, supervisors, branch specialists, program managers, operations officers and organizational problem solvers. Agencies need people in these grades who can walk into complexity, establish accountability, improve processes, train staff, coordinate across offices, communicate with leadership and sustain results. Senior NCOs already do this in large, mission-driven institutions. The Army’s “Be, Know, Do” framework offers a useful way to understand why senior NCO experience transfers so effectively. Senior NCOs bring the “Be” of public service values, integrity, stewardship and trust. They bring the “Know” of organizational systems, regulations, operations and human behavior within institutions. Most importantly, they bring the “Do” of execution, supervision, correction and measurable results. Federal agencies consistently say they need employees who can lead with character, understand complex systems and get things done. Senior NCOs arrive with all three. My own experience has confirmed this repeatedly. As a Command Sergeant Major in the California Army National Guard AGR program, I learned that readiness was never simply a report. It was a living system of people, records, training, evaluations, maintenance, inspections and follow-through. Later, as a program manager for the Army National Guard Distributed Learning Program at the National Guard Bureau, I saw how senior NCO competencies translated directly into federal-style program execution: enterprise coordination, stakeholder engagement, planning, resource management, training oversight and technology integration across all 54 states and territories. In my current role as a USDA division director, I continue to see that federal organizations need leaders who can make systems work every day, align staff and processes, improve workflows and sustain trust across organizational boundaries. These are not foreign demands to senior NCOs. They are familiar ones. One reason the federal government continues to miss this opportunity is that it struggles to translate military experience into civilian language. A senior NCO may have supervised operations, managed training systems, inspected compliance, coordinated logistics, advised senior leaders and improved organizational performance, yet still be screened out because their resume lacks civilian job titles familiar to human resources specialists. The issue is usually not lack of capability. It is failure to recognize functional equivalence. This problem affects the entire senior NCO population, not just one component. Active-duty and reserve-component senior NCOs alike often possess exactly the kind of specialized experience agencies claim to seek. They have led people, managed systems, maintained accountability and driven mission execution in organizations where failure has real consequences. They understand hierarchy, oversight, standards and adaptation. They know how to operate in environments where policy, leadership and execution must align every day. The federal government’s greatest overlooked resource is the U.S. military senior NCO corps itself. The central issue is not whether one subgroup is useful. It is whether agencies are willing to recognize that senior enlisted military leadership already develops many of the exact competencies required for civil service success at the GS-10 through GS-13 level. The concept of institutional readiness helps explain why. In the military, readiness is the ability of an organization to perform its mission now, sustained through training, maintenance, logistics, accountability, inspections and leader development. In civilian agencies, the language may change, but the need remains the same. An office is ready when its people are trained, its systems function, its records are current, its processes are clear, its standards are enforced and its leaders have reliable information. Senior NCOs understand instinctively that mission success depends on these underlying systems. They know that policy is only real when an organization can execute and sustain it. Sign up for our daily newsletter so you never miss a beat on all things federal If agencies want to correct this missed opportunity, they should begin by more deliberately recognizing senior NCO experience as qualifying experience for federal mid-level roles. Vacancy announcements should better reflect competencies such as inspections, readiness systems, training management, logistics integration, process improvement, supervision and cross-functional coordination. Hiring managers should be educated on what senior NCOs actually do. Transition pipelines should target senior enlisted leaders more intentionally. And agencies should stop assuming that senior NCOs must “start low” simply because their titles do not match familiar civilian labels. This is not an argument that military service should replace merit standards. It is an argument that the federal merit system should more accurately recognize the merit senior NCOs already possess. Public service requires leaders who can manage complexity, uphold standards, lead people and produce results in large organizations. Senior NCOs have already proven they can do exactly that. The federal government does not lack access to experienced, mission-oriented leaders prepared for GS-10 through GS-13 roles. It is already producing them through the U.S. military. The missed opportunity lies in failing to deliberately recognize, translate and place that talent where it can have the greatest effect. Senior NCOs are not simply veterans seeking a second career. They are institutional stewards trained to make large systems work under pressure. The question is no longer whether they can contribute on day one. The question is whether the federal government will hire them as though it truly understands their value. Sergio Porras is a retired U.S. Army Command Sergeant Major and is director of the TARGET Center at the Agriculture Department. Copyright

title: BMW F 450 GS Review: First Ride & Real-World Impressions - Team-BHP
content: The BMW F 450 GS is powered by an all-new 420 cc liquid-cooled parallel-twin engine. It uses a rather uncommon 135-degree crankshaft. For reference, the Honda NX 500 uses a 180-degree configuration, while the Royal Enfield 650 twins and Aprilia 457s use a 270-degree configuration. The engine produces 47 BHP @ 8,750 rpm and 43 Nm @ 6,750 rpm. According to BMW, 80% (35 Nm) of the torque is available from 3,000 rpm. The claimed top speed is 165 km/h. In our limited time with the motorcycle, we mostly rode on the narrow streets of Goa, along with a short ride on the four-lane highway that connects North Goa to South Goa. Before we get to the overall performance, let's first talk about the Easy Ride Clutch, also known as the ERC. It is essentially a mechanical system that combines a conventional multiplate clutch with a centrifugal clutch. It disengages at idle and engages as revs rise. You still have a physical clutch lever to override the ERC. You still need to shift gears manually, though, but the bi-directional quickshifter on offer means that you don't require much effort to do the same. Most quickshifters provide smoother upshifts at high revs. However, the F 450 GS's unit provides smooth upshifts in the mid-range as well. The only time you need to use the clutch lever is when starting the motorcycle. Once the engine comes to life, you can let go of the lever, and the bike won't stall. The ERC on the F 450 GS engages at 2,700 rpm. As the revs climb to this mark, the motorcycle starts moving ahead without any jerks as long as you are smooth with your throttle inputs. There are obvious benefits to this system, the most important being that you don't need to worry about operating the clutch lever in heavy traffic. Also, the motorcycle won't stall, irrespective of which gear you are in. That said, since it is a mechanical system with no electronic intervention, the motorcycle will try to move from a standstill even when you are in a higher gear. This could lead to overheating and excessive clutch wear in the long run. To prevent this, the TFT will display a pop-up message that reads "Select 1st gear to drive off!" to alert the rider. There are a few downsides to this system. For starters, when you come to a standstill on a slope and turn off the bike, the motorcycle will roll downwards even when it is in gear. There's no Hill Hold system to stop the bike from rolling back, nor do we have a manual handbrake. Hence, you need to be mindful about parking the motorcycle on a sloping surface. When riding off-road, beginner riders will appreciate not having to worry about modulating the clutch to avoid stalling. But in case you come to a halt on a steep slope with loose gravel or a slippery surface, rolling back down can become tricky. The whole clutchless riding experience takes some time to get used to. The initial throttle response, or rather the lack of it, until the ERC engages at 2,700 rpm, makes it seem like the engine lacks low-end grunt. Also, whenever the revs drop below 2,700 rpm, a pop-up message on the TFT recommends that you downshift. This feels intrusive and takes away from the enjoyment of riding a motorcycle. This is one of the reasons BMW should consider selling the 'Sport' variant in India, as it packs all the features of the Trophy trim except the ERC. The four ride modes on offer - Rain, Road, Enduro and Enduro Pro - alter the throttle response, traction control and ABS intervention, Wheel Lift Control, and Engine Drag Torque Control. On the narrow streets of Goa, the rain mode felt more than adequate. The throttle response, although soft, doesn't feel dull (above 2,700 rpm). Shifting to Road mode sharpens the throttle response and offers a more engaging riding experience. The overall power delivery is strong and linear, with a slight bump above 7,000 rpm; although it's not what we'd call particularly exciting. On our short ride on the four-lane highway of Goa, the F 450 GS felt comfortable cruising at highway speeds. 100 km/h comes at 5,500 rpm in the sixth gear, and there's a good amount of grunt on offer to make quick overtakes. We also briefly rode on an off-road trail where we tried out the Enduro and Enduro Pro ride modes. Given its torquey nature, it is easy to spin the rear wheel of the F 450 GS. In Enduro mode, the traction control lets you slide the rear wheel a bit before it kicks in. It engages smoothly and doesn't feel intrusive. Unlike the Enduro mode, which is optimised for standard tyres, the Enduro Pro mode has been tuned for off-road tyres, with traction control set to its minimal intervention setting. As a result, it is even easier to make the Maxxis tyre lose traction on loose gravel in this mode. Twin-cylinder engines are known to offer better refinement than single-cylinder engines, and the BMW F 450 GS's engine is no exception. However, the refinement levels are not as impressive as those of other similarly sized twin-cylinder engines in its category. Both bblost and I found the engine buzzy (for a twin-cylinder) at city speeds. You can feel the buzz via the fuel tank and seat base. It isn't harsh or jarring, but we'd expect a twin-cylinder bike to be smoother. Things improve as we move to highway speeds, though, as the engine feels relaxed at 100 km/h in sixth gear, @ 5,500 rpm. Another underwhelming aspect of the F 450 GS's parallel-twin engine is its sound. For starters, the exhaust note is not as deep and aurally pleasing as the Aprilia's 457 cc parallel-twin. Moreover, the engine noise drowns out the exhaust note. Its sound isn't the most refined either, which further dulls the overall aural experience. The BMW F 450 GS is underpinned by a tubular steel frame with the engine acting as a stressed member. There is a major focus on weight saving across the motorcycle. For starters, the engine weighs just around ~46kg, and the double-sided swingarm is made of hollow cast aluminium. As mentioned before, the standard alloys are made up of cast aluminium, too. As a result, the BMW F 450 GS weighs 178 kg, just ~8 kg more than the G 310 GS. On top of that, the weight management is excellent. One reason the F 450 GS is easy to manage despite its relatively tall seat is that it doesn't feel top-heavy. Suspension duties on the F 450 GS are handled by 43 mm KYB upside-down forks up front and a monoshock at the rear. The Base and the Exclusive trims come with non-adjustable front suspension, while the Trophy version features rebound and compression adjustability. The rear monoshock features preload and rebound adjustability, as well as progressive damping. There's 180 mm wheel travel on both ends. When we first received the motorcycle, the front tyre was over-inflated. The high temperatures in Goa didn't help either. As a result, I could feel every bump and ripple of the concrete road surface on the handlebar. Shortly after, we also had a puncture in the rear tyre from a nail. After fixing the same and reducing the tyre pressures in the front, things improved significantly. The suspension was absorbing the concrete road undulations much better, although there was a hint of firmness. On the tarmac, the F 450 GS glided over small bumps when riding at decent speeds. First impression: the damping feels plush (not Himalayan 450-level), but we'll reserve our final verdict on the suspension until we spend more time with the F 450 GS. The baby GS also impresses in the handling department. On the narrow, winding streets of Goa, the F 450 GS felt effortless to steer and was, in fact, a lot of fun to ride. On the long sweeping corners of the four-lane highway, the bike felt confident. It was eager to lean, but it took me some time to trust the block-pattern tyres to hold high lean angles. Braking on the F 450 GS is taken care of by a 310 mm disc coupled with a Brembo 4-piston calliper at the front and a 240 mm disc with a single-piston calliper at the rear. The setup offers excellent stopping power. The feedback from the front brake lever is sharp and confidence-inspiring. Even the rear brake lever provides decent feedback. It is easy to lock the rear wheel on a loose off-road surface. Speaking of ABS, there are two settings: Road and Off-Road. The former works in Rain and Road mode, while the latter is tuned for Enduro and Enduro Pro mode. Even at its maximum intervention setting in Rain and Road ride modes, it didn't feel intrusive or eager to intervene during hard braking. Keep yourself tuned in to the Indian automotive scene via Twitter, Youtube or RSS feeds.

title: Carolina Figueiredo GS named inaugural winner of Vera Rubin New Frontiers Prize - The Daily Princetonian
content: Physics graduate student Carolina Figueiredo GS won $50,000 as the inaugural laureate of the Breakthrough Prize Foundation’s Vera Rubin New Frontiers Prize on April 18. She was the sole recipient of the prize in its founding year, chosen for her Ph.D. research at Princeton that unearthed “hidden relations among quantum field theories.” The Breakthrough Prize Foundation, founded by Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and science philanthropist Yuri Milner among others in 2012, honors international researchers in the fundamental sciences. Figueiredo’s adviser Nima Arkani-Hamed, a visiting lecturer with the rank of professor at Princeton and professor at the Institute for Advanced Study, received a Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics himself in 2012. “I’m extremely happy and honored, and everything about being the inaugural winner, it’s amazing,” Figueiredo told The Daily Princetonian. “I was not expecting [it] at all. I didn’t even know of the existence of the prize, obviously, because it didn’t exist before.” The Vera Rubin prize specifically recognizes female physicists within two years following their Ph.D. Figueiredo, who came to Princeton in 2021, is graduating this year. Rubin was an American astronomer known for her work in confirming the presence of dark matter, and was awarded an honorary doctorate from Princeton in 2005. She was barred from Princeton’s astronomy program in the 1940s due to the University’s policy of not admitting women at the time. On the growing representation of women in the sciences, Figueiredo said, “As I see it, there’s been a growth of the number of women in science over the last two decades — more than that. It’s fantastic to have these extra recognitions, but besides that, you just start seeing it, and you don’t get to think so much about it.” Figueiredo received her bachelor’s degree at the Instituto Superior Técnico in Lisbon, Portugal. Since her undergraduate days, she “was always very obsessed with trying to understand things as simply as possible.” “I felt like that was something I tried during undergrad, and it became even more important that I kept trying to do that in my Ph.D.,” she added. Figueiredo’s awarded work began with something that looked, at first, like a coincidence. Her work began with three theories in particle physics that were previously believed disparate. However, she proved that all three were linked, each prohibiting the same set of particle collisions. “It was a whole semester of surprises,” Figueiredo said, recalling how the pattern emerged during her first year of Ph.D. research. She had initially noticed the vanishing probabilities in one simple theory, then tried to see if the same held for a second. It did. Then a third. She said she worked “out of curiosity, not with much hope that something would work out.” The explanation, which took until the winter of the winter of 2022 to develop, turned out to be geometric. All three theories share a single underlying mathematical structure: curves drawn on surfaces. This concept, now called surfaceology, can reproduce the predictions of conventional physics without ever tracking how individual particles move through space and time. Where the traditional approach relies on Feynman diagrams — intricate pictures that map out every possible way particles can interact across spacetime — surfaceology sidesteps that entirely, reaching the same answers through pure geometry. In conventional physics, spacetime is the stage where everything happens. Surfaceology suggests the stage might be optional. When asked whether she considers spacetime to be genuinely emergent or still speculative, Figueiredo pointed to a convergence of arguments from quantum mechanics and general relativity. Probing shorter distances requires higher energies, hence the enormity of experiments like CERN’s Large Hadron Collider. But gravity sets a hard limit: Concentrate enough energy into a small enough region and a black hole is formed. “Whatever is the most fundamental description,” she told the ‘Prince,’ “should become emergent in some way.” Arkani-Hamed has long pushed the emergent spacetime program forward. Surfaceology is among its sharpest concrete results. The new geometric framework of surfaceology currently applies to specific families of particles. Extending it to cover the full Standard Model, the complete inventory of particles and forces observed in nature, remains an open problem. “I cannot tell you exactly how [long] that will take,” Figueiredo said, “It is doable at least.” Following the announcement of the prize, she was congratulated by Portuguese President  António José Seguro for the prize. “Today is a day of pride for Portugal,” he wrote on Instagram in Portuguese. “Don’t be too concerned about not knowing everything,” Figueiredo said as advice for the future generation of fundamental scientists, “Because there’s a lot to know.” Daphne Lewis is a staff News writer for the ‘Prince.’ She is from Washington, D.C. and can be reached at dl1424[at]princeton.edu.
